11-018.r: Chandragupta II → killed his elder brother Ramagupta (who failed against the Sakas), married his wife Dhruv Devi and defeated the Sakas.

11-019.r: Huna invasions troubled the Gupta dynasty most; the first came under Skandagupta, who defeated the Hunas; they hastened Gupta decline.

11-024.r: Bhitari Pillar inscription (Saidpur tehsil, Ghazipur, UP) → records Skandagupta's war with and victory over the Hunas.
11-024.t: Allahabad pillar = Samudragupta; Mandsaur = Kumaragupta I; Bhitari = Skandagupta.

11-025.r: Not a cause of Gupta decline → Arab invasion (came in the medieval era). Causes: Huna invasions, feudal administration, later Guptas' acceptance of Buddhism.

11-026.r: Chandragupta II 'Vikramaditya' → 'Saka conqueror', title 'Sakari'; defeated last Saka king Rudrasimha III; first Gupta to issue silver coins (Rupak).

11-028.r: Chandragupta II's silver coins → strongest evidence of his Saka victory; they weighed about 30-33 grains. Both statements correct.

11-029.r: After conquering the Sakas (Gujarat, part of Malwa), Chandragupta II → took title 'Sakari' and issued dated silver coins.

11-030.r: Fa-hien (Chinese Buddhist monk, in India c. 399-412 CE) → visited during Chandragupta II's reign (c. 375-415 CE); did not meet the emperor.

11-032.r: Chandragupta II's daughter Prabhavati → married Vakataka king Rudrasena II; ruled the Vakataka kingdom as regent after his death.

11-033.r: Prabhavati Gupta (daughter of Chandragupta II) → Vakataka queen of Rudrasena II; ruled the Vakataka kingdom as regent after his death.
11-033.t: She was born a Gupta but ruled the Vakataka dynasty.

11-034.r: Pravarasena I (successor of Vindhyashakti) → real founder of Vakataka power; empire from Bundelkhand to Hyderabad (Deccan); called Pravira in Puranas. All statements correct.

11-035.r: Wrong pair: Udayagiri cave inscription → Chandragupta II, not Prabhavati Gupta. Correct: Mandsaur → Kumargupta I; Takshashila → Patik; Eran → Samudragupta.

11-036.r: Dashpur (Mandsaur) inscription of Kumaragupta I → called the world's first advertisement (about silk trade).

11-037.r: Mandsaur Prashasti (by Vatsabhatti, Malwa) → achievements of Kumaragupta I; silk workers built a Sun temple there, repaired by Bandhuvarma.

11-038.r: Dashpur (Mandsaur) inscription of Kumaragupta I → silk weavers' guild (Tantuwaya), governor Bandhuvarman and the Sun temple built by the guild.

11-039.r: Dashpur inscription → Lata (Gujarat) silk-weaver guild built the Sun Temple; oldest advertisement example; calls Dashpur 'Pashchimapur'; composed by Vatsabhatti, not Bhavabhuti.

11-040.r: Chandragupta I → Kumaradevi; Samudragupta → Duttadevi; Chandragupta II → Kubernaga; Kumaragupta I → Anantdevi.

11-041.r: Gupta administrative divisions, large to small → Bhukti (province, under Uparika), Vishaya (Vishayapati), Vithi, Grama (village).

11-042.r: After the Huna invasion ended the Roman Empire (3rd century AD), Indian merchants relied more on South-East Asian trade.

11-043.r: Tamralipti (Bengal) → Gupta port for North Indian trade and links with South-East Asia, China, Lanka, Java, Sumatra; Bhrigukachchha (Bharuch) → west-coast port for western trade.

11-044.r: Gupta-era ports for North Indian trade → Tamralipti (most important) plus Bharuch, Kalyan and Cambay; so 'more than one' (e).
11-044.t: IAS asked the same with answer Tamralipti; with option (e) present, the book picks (e).

11-045.r: India's early sea links with South-East Asia across the Bay of Bengal → explained by monsoon winds that eased sea voyages.

11-046.r: Ancient guilds (Shreni) → fixed wages, work rules, standards and prices; held judicial power over members; worked under royal recognition but not run by the king. Statements 2, 3 correct.

11-047.r: Gujarat, Bengal, Deccan and Tamil country (Gupta period) → textile manufacture centres; textiles were the prime industry.

11-048.r: Sarthavaha (Srenipramukh, head of trade guild) → linked with the Vaishya varna; trade rules called Samay and Srenidharma.

11-049.r: No listed person did Gupta-era medicine: Sushruta (father of surgery, Kashi, c. 600 BC) is far earlier; Shaunaka was a Rigvedic sage; Shudraka, Saumilla were Gupta dramatists.
11-049.t: BPSC's first key said Sushruta; the book rejects it, as Sushruta lived about 875 years before the Guptas.

11-051.r: Not linked to medicine → Bhaskaracharya (astronomer-mathematician; Siddhanta Shiromani, Lilavati). Dhanvantari (Chandragupta II's Navratna), Charaka, Sushruta → Ayurveda.

11-053.r: True: surgical instruments common by 1st century AD; sine known in 5th century AD (Surya Siddhanta, Aryabhatiya); cyclic quadrilaterals by Brahmagupta (700 AD). False: organ transplants.

11-054.r: Fa-Hien → described a hospital at Pataliputra, endowed by citizens, giving free care, food and medicine to poor patients.

11-055.r: Chandragupta II's Nine Gems: Kshapanak → astrologer; Kalidasa poet; Dhanvantari physician; Varahamihira astronomer; Amar Simha lexicographer; Shanku architect; Vararuchi grammarian.

11-057.r: Aryabhatta (Aryabhatiyam) → first said day and night are caused by Earth's rotation on its axis.

11-058.r: Gupta gold coins → Dinara; Fa Hien says people used Dinara for daily business.

11-060.r: Gupta silver coins → Rupaka; most Gupta coins found at Bayana (Bharatpur, Rajasthan).

11-061.r: First Gupta ruler to issue coins → Chandragupta I; no coins known from Srigupta or Ghatotkacha.

11-062.r: Gupta-period Sanskrit plays → women and Sudras speak Prakrit; upper-varna characters speak Sanskrit.

11-063.r: First inscriptional evidence of Sati → Eran inscription (510 AD), wife of war commander Gopraj.

11-064.r: Gupta Samvat → started by Chandragupta I in 319 AD.

11-065.r: Ashoka → Priyadarsin; Samudragupta → Parakramanka; Chandragupta II → Vikramaditya; Skandagupta → Kramaditya.
11-065.t: Vikramaditya (Chandragupta II) vs Kramaditya (Skandagupta): look-alike titles.

11-066.r: Gradual decline of towns → Gupta period; Pataliputra was a village by Hiuen-Tsang's visit; Mathura, Hastinapur, Sravasti also declined.

11-067.r: Gupta dynasty → donated the most villages to temples and Brahmins.

11-068.r: Gupta rule → 'Golden Age' of ancient India for its excellence in art and culture.

11-069.r: Women never had equality with men in Gupta, Mauryan or Chola ages (only the Vedic age was better) → 'None of these'.

11-070.r: Gupta land revenue → one-sixth of produce; called 'Udranga' and 'Bhag' in Gupta inscriptions.

11-071.r: Religious texts (Hindu law) → valid land revenue is 1/6 of the produce.

11-073.r: Aprahat → uncultivated forest land; a Gupta-period revenue term.

11-074.r: Kulyavapa and Dronavapa → units of land measurement in the Gupta period.

11-075.r: Gupta Empire → granted tax-free agrarian land to Brahmins (religious functionaries).

11-076.r: Udakabhaga → irrigation tax; Hiranya → cash tax (Mauryan); Udranga → land tax (Gupta inscriptions); Uparnika → tax on farmers living on the land.
11-076.h: Udaka = water, so Udakabhaga = water (irrigation) share.

11-077.r: Araghatta → large wheel with earthen pots tied to its spokes (Ar = spokes, Ghata = pot); water-lifting device known as the Persian wheel.

11-078.r: Warangal (3rd century AD) → famous for iron implements; made by the Agaria people.

11-079.r: Ghantasala, Kadura and Chaul (Gupta period) → ports handling foreign trade.

11-080.r: Toramana → Huna; leader of the second Huna invasion of India.

11-081.r: Huna ruler Mihirakula → defeated by Aulikara king Yashodharman of Malwa (528 AD; some sources say 495 AD).

11-082.r: Chinese traveller Sungyun → in India 518-521 AD collecting Buddhist texts; none of the given ranges fit, so (e).

11-083.r: Chinese pilgrim who visited India in the early 6th century → Sungyun.
11-083.t: Fa-hien came earlier (Chandragupta II); Hiuen Tsang (Ywan Chwang) and I-tsing came later.

11-084.r: Sri Lankan king Meghavarman → sent a mission to Samudragupta, who allowed him to build a Buddhist monastery at Bodh Gaya.

11-085.r: Gupta kings → claimed divine (supernatural) origin and extended land grants; administration not centralised but federal. Statements 1 and 3 true.

11-086.r: Vishti (forced labour, Gupta period) → a sort of tax and state income, unpaid; Junagadh inscription shows it in Gujarat-Malwa.

11-087.r: Chess → originated in India in the Gupta period as 'Chaturanga'; reached Iran and then Europe.

11-088.r: Shudraka's 'Mrichchhakatika' (The Little Clay Cart) → love of a rich merchant and a courtesan's daughter; shows Gupta society and Shudra officers in Ujjayini.

11-089.r: Sankhya Darshan → propounded by Maharshi Kapila, its 'Acharya'; he wrote 'Sankhya Sutra' and Tattvasamas.

11-092.r: Sankhya → accepts rebirth (statement 1 false); self-knowledge, not any outside agent, leads to liberation (statement 2 true).

11-093.r: Kapila → earliest exponent of Sankhya; teaches man's life is shaped by forces of nature, not divine agency. Both statements true.

11-094.r: Satkaryavada (effect pre-exists in its cause) → main doctrine of Sankhya philosophy.

11-095.r: Yoga Darshan → propounded by Maharshi Patanjali as a compact philosophy ('Patanjali Darshan'); yoga ideas also in Upanishads, Mahabharata, Gita.

11-097.r: Ashtanga Yoga's Antaranga Sadhana → last three limbs Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi. Eight limbs: Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama, Pratyahara, Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi; Anusmriti not one.
11-097.h: Inner three = D-D-S: Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi.

11-099.r: Patanjali, author of Mahabhashya → contemporary of Pushyamitra Shunga (184-148 BC).
